From: Mr. G.A. Matthews, Essex

Dear Sir,

DRIVECHAT'S Atari interference
suppressors are called toroid
rings and are obtainable from
TANDY for `1.99 each. Loop your
aerial lead through the ring as
many times as you can.TANDY also
do an R.F. filter. If you live
near a citizen band radio maniac
like I do you soon become an
expert on the subject.

I have had a total disaster. I
subscribe to several Spectrum
user groups-SPECTRUM PROGRAMMER,
DATABASE. I was outraged by an
editorial in DATABASE. I shall
not renew my subscription.I sent

the complete berk that edits it
a tape with a Tasword file and
2 short programs to demonstrate
my point;the disaster being that
although I labelled the tape:
"TASWORD FILE DISPLAY 1 AND 2"
he played the rest of the tape
which I had been using to trans-
fer some items from OUTLET to
disk from microdrive. This berk
seemed to conclude they were my
work. I have written to him
telling him they are definitely
not mine and not to use them.
I'm sorry it happened.

Odd bits and pieces: On +3 type:
OUT 32765,21, press ENTER and
you're in "Spectrum mode". Type:
OUT 32768,48 and you're in the
original 48K mode.

By the way, with reference to a
much earlier item in OUTLET
about using contact spray to
clean edge contacts, I recently
had a nasty experience with
TANDY's contact cleaner, a prod-
uct I would normally thoroughly
recommend. At work, I sprayed a
Honeywell control panel with it,
which is really a dedicated com-
puter controlling an industrial
robot. I intended to clean oxide
deposits from the connections.
Some of the spray went over the
PC board. The effect was that
several components simply
dropped over then fell out. Boy,
was I in trouble. Moral: be
careful where you spray it.

                - G.A. Matthews

To: Mr. G.A. Matthews from Brian

Gulp! I've just started using a
contact spray on the edge
connectors of my two Spectrums!

Thanks for the various bits of
info. You mentioned a bit of
code (which I regret we can't
use in OUTLET as it's copyright)
and that you have a dodgy drive
you're giving away so I'll
change your OUTBOARD message.

Don't worry about the DATABASE
mix-up. Are they connected with
the old Buccaneer group? I've an
idea I saw an advert with the
same address. I've done a short
review of SPECTRUM PROGRAMMER in
CHECKOUT this issue.   - Brian

From:Don Weerasinghe,London,W12.

Many thanks for OUTLET 9 and the
BONABANNER cartridge. BONABANNER
is marvellous and really good
value for money.I am experiment-
ing and getting the hang of how
to use it and hope to send you
my artistic output one of these
days. A useful addition would
have been a HELP menu as is
available in TASWORD. I expect
once one gets familiar with the
controls it will become easier.

I attended the ZX Microfair on
the 11th June but this time not
as a visitor but volunteered to
help Mike as an assistant. As
you're aware, Mike Johnston runs
the ZX Microfair with the help

of his Dad and a band of dedi-
cated hardworking helpers. I
really enjoyed the show and had
a little time to pick up a few
bargains. There was quite a good
attendance right through the
day. Why didn't OUTLET come?

I met one of your keen Outlett-
ers who went out of his way to
meet Mike and express his appre-
ciation of the ZXM. He learnt
about it from your message in
LOOKOUT, Issue 9. He wanted to
know when the next show would be
as he travels up from Devon. I
told him I would request Mike to
inform OUTLET who will, I am
sure, advertise it in the issue
before the show.
               - Don Weerasinghe


To Don Weerasinghe from Brian

Thanks, Don. We can't even find
time to visit the ZXM let alone
have a stand again! I wish we
could but I'm sure you'd rather
we spend the day(and the days of
preparation) producing the next
OUTLET. We'll certainly advise
readers of the date of the next
ZXM.
                - Brian

From Pat Cleary, Harlow

Dear Sirs,

Thanks for a speedy reply to my
request for a copy of your
sampler magazine, which I hasten
to add, impressed me no end.

I write (type?) in the hope that
your good selves or another
reader can help me out with a
minor problem I've been trying
to sort out for some time now.

I purchased a copy of THE WRITER
because it could be transferred
to a microdrive cartridge. Now
the Plus D (which I am fortunate
enough to own) understands the
M'drive syntax so I assumed I

could transfer the program to
disc- and to a certain extent my
assumption was correct. However
after the first ten blocks have
loaded a 'Stream used' message
appears and any further trans-
ferring to disc ends. I've en-
closed a copy of the BASIC load-
er for blocks ten onwards and if
you can suggest any admendments
in order to solve my problem I
would apreciate it.

I've another query regarding THE
WRITER and that is printing - to
put it simply I can't. I own a
ZX +2 and a Brother HR-5 plugged
straight into the +2's RS232
port, but the printer install
program doesn't appear to cater
for this combination. If anyone


has come up against this problem
and overcome it I'd be pleased
to hear from them.

I also experience problems when
it comes to printing using
Outlet. If I load the sampler
using the loader option on my +2
then I can print using the
Kempston E option. If I load
using the 48K mode however, and
again use the Kempston E option,
nothing happens.Any suggestions?
What's more, if I do use the
Kempston E option all I get is a
copy of the Jotter title screen
and not my letter as hoped.

Lastly(was that a sigh of relief
I heard)I notice that Outlet was
designed for the 48K Spectrum as

amongst other things Jig Blox
won't work in 128K mode. Do you
intend releasing a 128K version?
Thanking you for your co-oper-
ation,
                Pat Cleary.

To: Patrick Cleary from Ron


Dear Pat,

Re your query with "The Writer".
Another reader, Bill Clark, has
also had problems with printing
with this word processer. As he
had tried writing to Softechnics
without success, I offered to
look at the program to see if
there was a solution that we
could implement. Unfortunately,
just after that, the serial
interface on my printer refused
to work so I was unable to do
much testing. For the last two
or three months I have been
printing via the Disciple disk
interface but the few attempts I

have had with "The Writer" have
failed. The main problem is that
the program is entirely written
in machine code and it is very
much more difficult to hack into
to find the print routines etc.

To be honest, I find it one of
the most exasperating programs I
have come across. I have now
tried four different Word
Processer programs and they all
have this effect on me - all bar
Tasword Two which I use every
day - but "The Writer" is
particularly bad. I have yet to
find out how to load in a text
file! The only files I have been
able to load are those that are
automatically pulled in by the
Help command.

Incidentally, you can save the
main program with the Plus D's
Snapshot button and save a file
or do a catalogue, so I assume
it must be possible to run it
from disk - it just needs the
printer problem ironing out!

Anyhow, I suggest the fault lies
with the program and not your
printer/interface combination
but I hope by printing this
letter that there may be other
readers - who have had more
success with it than we have -
and can explain how to install a
straight-forward Epson-type
printer.

With regard to your printing
from OUTLET. I can't figure out
what is happening here - I know

other readers are using the
Kempston system successfully -
if you are printing the Jotter
title page, you are getting a
screen dump from somewhere. Did
you also get a screen dump when
attempting to print the normal
text pages in OUTLET?

Most of the Kempston commands
use the COPY token but does the
128K also respond to this as did
the ZX and Alphacom printers? If
it does then that would explain
the screen dump, but I would
have thought that the text would
still have printed after that
(even if incorrectly justified).
But this doesn't explain why it
would not work in 48K mode - are
you sure you have the "E" type
Kempston and not the "S" (which

requires some code to be loaded)
- alternatively, does anyone
know if Kempston have produced
an interface using different
syntax?

Following on to your last point,
Pat, it is unlikely that we will
bring out a 128K version of
OUTLET as, although there is
more memory within the computer,
there would be insufficient
space on the cartridges - I
calculate that a typical OUTLET,
written in memory-hungry 128K
Basic, would occupy at least 3
cartridges.

So there you have it. None out
of three - how did you manage
without us before now!
                       - Ron

To: J.N. Burke from Brian

I'd like to reply as the KAYCAT
problem may affect other users.

The fault is mine as I added a
CLEAR # in the wrong place. The
problem is I still have not got
a printer lead for the Opus and
so can't test print options. The
solution to KAYCAT is to move
the CLEAR # from the start of
line 80 to the start of line 70.
(i.e. BREAK in, EDIT line 80,
DELETE the CLEAR #, EDIT line 70
and add CLEAR #: at the start)
Enter RUN 9980 to ERASE and RE-
SAVE the program.

Glad you liked ARNOLD which uses
a BASIC pixel move (OUT-TAKE 1)!
                       - Brian

From: John Luby,  Duns,

Dear Ron/Brian,

Aaaarghh!!! I checked that BIN
thing -you're right! (Which is
NO excuse -I've used it all over
the place!) You can't trust the
Spectrum an inch, can you?

Outlet keeps getting better and
better, especially with the
utility items. Can I suggest
some future utilities? How about
machine-code sort routines, an
'instring' search routine, a
(really good) renumber facility,
or a routine to "grab" screens
as well as put them back.

Many thanks to David Gent -I

used to have a note of the 128
renumber POKEs, but lost it a
while ago. I didn't have that
block delete tip of G.A.
Matthews either, -well done G.A.

I liked Paul Hiley's LIFE
program. It's an old favourite,
but Paul's version is better
than most.

Harking back to HANDYWIDE, I've
found a further use for
"minichars" as an alternate
character set for Tasword 2.
It's not quite that easy, as the
minichar letters are on the left
of the character cell, and
Tasword characters are on the
right (which is why the Tasword
char set doesn't work with

HANDYWIDE either). Most good
font editors can shift them
over. If you haven't got one, I
enclose one of my own making,
although I've never met a
serious Spectrum user who didn't
have at least one. Tasword looks
quite different with the
slightly larger character set.
Load it at address 61184 for
Tasword 2.

For the growing number of
128'ers (and +2'ers and +3'ers),
can I expand on Paddy Mulcahy's
screen edit key tip with (I
think!) the full list of keys:

<E> N : goto start of program.
<G> W :   "    "   "     "

<E> T : goto end of program.
<G> V :   "   "  "     "
<ES>2 : goto start of line.
<G> Y :   "    "   "   "
<E> M : goto end of line.
<G> X :   "   "  "   "
<ES>8 : switch screen mode.
<G> Z :    "      "    "
<E> P : go up half page.
<S> I : go down half page.
<ES>J : goto next word.
<E> I : goto previous word.
<E> E : delete previous word.
<E> J : delete to end of line.
<E> K : delete to start of line.
<E> W : delete to end of word.
<ES>K : delete this character

 <G> = GRAPHIC MODE
 <E> = EXTEND MODE
 <S> = SYMBOL SHIFT
<ES> = EXTEND MODE +SYMBOL SHIFT

All of the 'keypad' controls
seem to be there, although some
are more trouble than they're
worth! On the subject of the
vanished keypad, any hardware
buffs out there up to designing
a home-made one? Or ANY ideas at
all on possible uses for that
'keypad' socket? I can't see
that Amstrad have any moral
right to grumble, seeing as how
they chickened out!

Back to the subject of PROCs,
structure, etc: I don't think we
disagree about all that much,
Brian. I DO think, though, that
while a structured program
rarely develops from an
unstructured start, it doesn't
automatically result from the
.

reverse either, and any
programming tool that makes the
development process easier has
got to be a good thing. Outlet
programs usually prove both our
points, but I've seen some real
horrors out of supposedly
professional software houses!
Utilities like BetaBasic don't
(as you rightly point out)
automatically structure your
programs for you, but
programming with devices like
DO...LOOP and PROCs does at
least teach you that there are
more elegant forms of program
design than a host of GOTOs.

A final item in reply to John
Taylor's recent SHOUTBURST on
violence and software:

Sorry John, but I think that
there's an "us and them" aspect
to your argument that could
ultimately be as dangerous as
the problem we're discussing.


I agree that it is wrong to
teach kids, directly or
indirectly, that violence is a
simple answer to life's
problems, or that the consequ-
ences in real life are ever as
neat as they are in films and
games. However, we're not just
talking of children, and it's
facile simply to divide society
into the us (goodies) and them
(baddies) -isn't that the kind
of attitude we're blaming the
programmers and film-makers for?

EVERYONE has a tendency to
violence, and how many of us, if
we're honest, cannot recall some
situation which, if it had
developed differently, could not
have led to violence -on OUR
part! If that isn't true, please
send me the address of the
monastery you live in! I've met
more than a few highly intelli-
gent, well-off and TOTALLY
amoral people, and the formative
factors aren't always that easy
to determine.

There ISN'T some 'bad' section
of society bent on violence
against the rest of us. The
non-violent among us are perhaps
those fortunate enough not to
have been driven to it too

often, or are we anti-social in
other, more subtle, but equally
immoral, ways? Do glossy
American soap-operas with their
tacky values encourage even a
few immature people to resort to
dishonesty to achieve a certain
life-style? If so, should we ban
them?

There ARE people who take
pleasure in violence, and we
read of them every day, but I
think we're then talking of
psychopathy rather than lack of
intelligence, and the predelict-
ion of such people for violent
films, etc., is the RESULT of
their condition and outlook, NOT
the cause.

There ARE films, books and
software that leave a very bad
taste indeed in MY mouth, but
that's a personal attitude and I
have no right to expect others
to share it. It has always been
too easy to censor on the basis
that "of COURSE it doesn't do ME
any harm, but what of ORDINARY
people?". I want to be free to
read and view as I please,
without my choice being limited
by the specious argument that
some small percentage of the
population COULD, PERHAPS, be
turned on to violence by the
media in question. We could ban
anything and everything on that
basis!

What should be available to


minors is, of course another
matter, and one which could
better be dealt with on a more
positive basis of what IS made
available than what ISN'T. I
used to have great hopes of the
potential of adventure games,
for instance. But that's another
argument... (hopefully!)

So there!

            Cheers,

             John Luby.

To John Luby from Brian

I have added to my projects list
a m/code sort and search. I've
already got some routines I may
be able to adapt.There's a BASIC
re-number in TK50 in Issue 11
but what I would like to see is
one that can do selected areas
(including any using VAL"" which
I use a lot) and even move them
to other areas of the program
OVER intervening areas, e.g. to
renumber 1500 to 1700 and put it
at 5500 to 5700. I have that on
my list! Grabbing SCREEN$ and
restoring them instantly when
needed is quite easy in machine
code and you might care to study
OUTCLASS this issue which has
such a routine. Once you see the


principle of it you can, with a
bit of thought, write routines
yourself to store just a third
of a screen or just the colours
or store several screens.

I'm determined to try minichars
in Tasword - I haven't had a
chance yet but it sounds like a
good idea. Ta.

I absolutely agree with all your
comments on violence.

I STILL have great hopes for
adventures! I have a dream that
one day there will be... No! no
room here for ALL I want to say
on that subject!
                       - Brian

minors is, of course another matter, and one which could better be dealt with on a more positive basis of what IS made available than what ISN'T. I used to have great hopes of the potential of adventure games, for instance. But that's another argument... (hopefully!)
